blocks.text: **Windows** is an operating system made by **Microsoft**. It is mainly **proprietary software** (the source code is not freely open). Its first version, **Windows 1.0**, appeared on **20 November 1985** as a graphical environment running on top of **MS-DOS**.

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: Graphical User Interface - windows, icons, menus and buttons that you use with a mouse, keyboard or touch.
Running several applications in one session at the same time.
New Technology - the family that all modern desktop Windows versions belong to.
The kernel of modern NT-based Windows is commonly classified as **hybrid**.

blocks.title: What Windows supports
items: A visual GUI with mouse, keyboard and touch input
Installing compatible third-party software on desktops and laptops (subject to permissions)
Windows 10 came in both 32-bit and 64-bit editions; **Windows 11 is 64-bit only** but can run many compatible 32-bit applications

blocks.title: Windows vs open-source systems
rows: Proprietary OS from Microsoft; NT family with a hybrid kernel
A Linux **distribution** (a complete OS built around the Linux kernel)
Its core is open source through **AOSP**; devices can also ship proprietary apps and drivers

blocks.title: The first operating system
blocks.text: **GM-NAA I/O**, used on the **IBM 704 in 1956**, is commonly cited as the first operating system. It was developed by **General Motors Research** and **North American Aviation** and improved **batch processing**. Use this proper name, not vague labels such as GMOS.

blocks.title: Important exact dates
rows: 24 August 1995 - Windows Explorer and My Computer arrived with this version
Business availability in 2006; worldwide consumer launch on 30 January 2007
14 October 2025 (extended-security and specialised editions have separate terms)

blocks.title: Historical exam facts
items: **Windows 8** removed the traditional desktop Start button.
**Windows 2000 Professional** was a client edition; the Server editions supported server roles.

blocks.title: Do not mix the 2021 dates
blocks.text: Windows 11 has three dates: **unveiled 24 June**, **availability date announced 31 August**, **general release 5 October 2021**. Only 5 October is the release. Likewise, Vista has two years: 2006 (business) and 2007 (consumer).

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: The two 2000s: **Windows 2000** (business, NT-based) and **Windows ME** (home) were both released in 2000. First Windows 1985, Explorer 1995, Windows 11 in 2021.

blocks.title: Desktop basics
rows: The main workspace you see after signing in.
Usable desktop space, excluding the taskbar and other reserved desktop toolbars.
The background image or colour behind desktop items.
Gives access to apps, search, files, settings and power options such as Restart or Shut down.

blocks.title: Taskbar and system tray
items: **Taskbar** buttons launch pinned apps and switch between running windows.
A **minimized** app usually keeps running; its taskbar button restores it.
The taskbar is **not** a storage location.
**System tray = notification area**, normally at the right end of a horizontal taskbar. It can show network, volume, battery, security, printing and background-app status.
The clock and date sit in the taskbar's system area.

blocks.title: Tray traps
blocks.text: **Microsoft Office Suite** is not a standard system-status indicator. **Action Center** is a separate panel, not another name for the system tray.

blocks.title: Taskbar position depends on the version
rows: Can sit on any screen edge
Stays at the bottom; its icons can align left or centre

blocks.title: Title bar buttons
rows: Usually shows the app or document name.
Hides the window but keeps it open.
Returns the window to its earlier size.
Closes the window; an unsaved-work prompt may appear. Shortcut: Alt + F4.

blocks.text: **Windows Explorer**, now called **File Explorer**, is Microsoft's graphical **file manager**, introduced with **Windows 95**. It browses files, folders, drives and network locations, and supports copy, move, rename, search and delete.

blocks.title: Ways to open it
items: Click its pinned folder icon on the taskbar
Type **explorer** or **explorer.exe** in the Run box (do not type the shortcut text Windows + E into Run)

blocks.title: File Explorer window, top to bottom
items: File commands; design varies by Windows version
Current path; search the chosen location
Left pane, main area, right pane

blocks.title: Explorer window parts
rows: On the **LEFT** side; browse folders, drives, libraries, OneDrive and network locations.
Convenient access to pinned or recent locations; labels vary by version.
The main area showing items in the selected location; it is not the navigation pane.
File commands; design varies by Windows version.
Shows a preview of the content.
Shows information about the selected item.

blocks.title: Eight common folder views
rows: Columns such as Name, Type, Size and Date modified

blocks.text: Win + E opens File Explorer. The navigation pane is on the left. There are **8** common folder views.

blocks.title: Everyday file actions
rows: Select the item and press **F2**, or right-click and choose Rename
**Ctrl + Shift + N**, type a name, press Enter
Normally sends eligible local items to the **Recycle Bin**

blocks.title: Recycle Bin limits
blocks.text: Shift + Delete bypasses the Recycle Bin but does **not** guarantee secure erasure or prevent recovery. The Recycle Bin can restore many deleted items until it is emptied; some locations and deletion methods bypass it.

blocks.title: Filename rules
items: Nine characters cannot normally appear in a filename: backslash \, forward slash /, colon :, asterisk *, question mark ?, double quote ", less-than <, greater-than > and pipe |.
Ordinary names should not end with a space or a period.
Reserved device names include **CON, PRN, AUX and NUL**.
My Documents / Documents is a common default working folder; the real Open and Save locations depend on the app and user settings.

blocks.title: Filename vs full path
rows: **260 characters** including the terminating null - it is the whole-path limit, not the filename limit.
Windows 10 version 1607 and later can support them when the required settings and application support are present.

blocks.text: A **file system** organises stored files and folders on a drive. It is **not a document format**. **NTFS (New Technology File System)** was introduced with **Windows NT 3.1 in 1993** and is normally used for the system partition of modern Windows. NT-based releases support it: 2000, XP, Vista, 7, 8, 10 and 11.

blocks.title: Important NTFS features
rows: Records file-system changes to help recovery.
Control which users can access files.
Can reduce the stored file size.
Encrypting File System - encrypts individual files on NTFS.
Transactional NTFS, introduced with Vista; lets certain file operations succeed or fail as one unit. Microsoft recommends alternatives for new development.

blocks.text: A file cannot use ordinary **NTFS compression** and **EFS encryption** at the same time.

blocks.title: Other file systems
rows: Supported by Windows for appropriate uses
Supported by Windows for appropriate uses
Linux - not a standard native File Explorer file system
Apple systems - not a standard native File Explorer file system

blocks.title: What the limit means
blocks.text: These numbers concern **incoming resource-sharing or device connections**. They do not mean 20 simultaneous desktop users or 20 open files.

blocks.title: Networking in older Windows
items: A **client-server network** uses servers to supply services and resources; **Windows 2000 Server** editions supported these roles.
Standard **Windows 3.1** lacked integrated networking; add-on software could provide it.

blocks.title: Startup modes
rows: The default; loads configured drivers, services and the desktop
Loads only a limited set of essential files and drivers, for troubleshooting
Safe Mode plus networking drivers and services
Uses a command window instead of the usual desktop

blocks.title: Not a real mode
blocks.text: **Turbo Mode** is not a standard Windows startup mode. Command Prompt alone is an application; the startup option is Safe Mode with Command Prompt.

blocks.title: Opening advanced startup
rows: Press **F8** before Windows loads to get Advanced Boot Options
Hold **Shift** while selecting Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings

items: The Windows Boot Manager selects and starts the operating-system loader; the loader starts the kernel with the required components.
**NTLDR** belongs to older systems such as Windows XP.
**explorer.exe** provides the desktop shell later; it is not the initial boot manager.
The claim that bootmgr always loads first needs BIOS/UEFI and Windows-version context.

blocks.title: Built-in protection
rows: Filters **network traffic** by security rules and helps block unauthorised connections.
Separate profiles, settings and permissions; passwords and other sign-in methods restrict access. Managed through Settings and Control Panel tools.

blocks.title: Encryption and recovery tools
rows: Rolls back system files, drivers, Registry settings and certain installed software using restore points

blocks.title: Encryption is not backup, restore is not file backup
blocks.text: Encryption protects **confidentiality**; it does not make a spare copy. System Restore is for **system recovery**, not a personal-file backup, and it differs from restoring a deleted document from the Recycle Bin. Encryption availability depends on the Windows edition and device configuration.

blocks.title: Third-party security: Bitdefender
items: Bitdefender is a developer of antivirus and other security products.
**Bitdefender Antivirus Free for Windows** is a free malware-protection tier; other editions are paid.
**Safepay** is its specialised secure-browsing feature, associated with sensitive tasks such as online banking; availability depends on the product.
Do not describe every Bitdefender product as fully free, or as mainly for online banking.

blocks.text: Windows uses a **paging file**, usually **pagefile.sys**, as part of **virtual-memory** management. It stores some memory pages outside physical RAM. It is not a substitute for RAM, because disk storage is much slower than RAM.

blocks.title: Configuration tools
rows: A hierarchical database of many Windows, app and user settings.
Command that opens the Registry Editor.
Command that opens the Services console, to view service status and manage startup settings.

blocks.title: Task Manager and cleanup
items: **Task Manager** monitors running apps and processes, resource use and system performance.
It can close an unresponsive process; shortcut **Ctrl + Shift + Esc**.
**Disk Cleanup** removes selected temporary and unnecessary files to free storage.
**Optimize Drives / defragmentation** is about storage optimisation, not deleting junk files.

blocks.title: Command Prompt and key folders
rows: Executable **cmd.exe**; runs text commands for listing, copying and changing files and system tasks.
Holds essential Windows executables, libraries, drivers and configuration components. Typical path: **C:\Windows\System32** (the installation drive may differ).

blocks.title: Command cheat line
blocks.text: regedit = Registry, services.msc = Services, cmd.exe = Command Prompt, explorer.exe = File Explorer.

blocks.title: Windows 11 interface
items: Redesigned **Start menu** and **centred taskbar icons** by default.
**Widgets** show information such as weather and news.
**Virtual desktops** organise apps into separate workspaces.
Launch highlights included **Microsoft Teams Chat** integration and gaming technologies such as **Auto HDR** and **DirectStorage** on compatible hardware.

blocks.title: Snap and shake
rows: Resizes and positions selected windows at screen edges or corners.
Suggests other windows to fill the remaining spaces.
Predefined arrangements in Windows 11; hover over Maximize or press **Win + Z**. Six layouts appear on some displays, but choices depend on screen size and orientation.
Minimizes other windows when you shake the active title bar. Turn it on in Settings > System > Multitasking.
Also minimizes or restores other windows.

blocks.title: Sticky Keys
rows: An accessibility feature that lets you use modifier-key combinations one key at a time.
Press **Shift five times** when enabled; Windows may ask for confirmation.

blocks.title: Former features
items: **Cortana** was Microsoft's digital assistant in Windows 10 and earlier Windows 11 releases; its standalone Windows app was retired in 2023.
Selected Android apps once ran through the **Windows Subsystem for Android** and the **Amazon Appstore**; support for that arrangement ended on **5 March 2025**, so treat it as a former feature.

blocks.title: Windows logo key (Win) shortcuts
rows: Snap the window to that side
Minimize or restore other desktop windows

blocks.title: Other essential keys
rows: Close the active window or app
Refresh the desktop or a supported active window

blocks.text: Win means the Windows logo key. Shortcut behaviour can depend on the app and the Windows version.

blocks.title: Text and document tools
rows: Plain-text editor; commonly works with .txt files.
Basic formatted-document editor formerly bundled with Windows; removed starting with **Windows 11 version 24H2**, so it is a historical answer in older exams.

blocks.title: Browser vs search engine
rows: Microsoft's modern browser supplied with Windows 10/11
Microsoft's earlier browser, predecessor to Edge - not the world's first browser

items: A **browser** displays web pages; a **search engine** finds information online.
The older Windows XP question expects **MSN** in its historical Internet Explorer / MSN Search context.
Browser search providers can be changed.

blocks.title: Refresh vs hard reload (Chrome on Windows)
rows: Shift + F5 or Ctrl + Shift + R

blocks.text: A hard reload bypasses cached content for that one reload; it does **not** erase the entire browser cache.

blocks.title: Last-minute reminders
items: A GUI uses visual controls; Command Prompt runs text commands.
The **clipboard** stores copied or cut content; icons represent items; thumbnails preview contents.
Disk Cleanup removes unnecessary files; BitLocker encrypts drives.
Normal startup is the default; Safe Mode is for troubleshooting.

revision: Windows is Microsoft's mainly proprietary GUI operating system; Windows 1.0 came on 20 November 1985 over MS-DOS.
NT = New Technology; XP = eXPerience; Windows 11 is 64-bit only.
GM-NAA I/O (IBM 704, 1956) is commonly cited as the first operating system.
Explorer and My Computer arrived with Windows 95 (public launch 24 August 1995).
Windows 11: unveiled 24 June 2021, general release 5 October 2021; Windows 10 standard support ended 14 October 2025.
Windows 8 removed the Start button, 8.1 restored it, and Windows 10 brought back a redesigned Start menu.
System tray = notification area; Minimize keeps the app running; Alt + F4 closes the active window.
File Explorer: Win + E; navigation pane on the left; 8 common folder views; Run command explorer.exe.
F2 renames, Ctrl + Shift + N makes a new folder, Alt + Enter opens Properties, Shift + Delete bypasses the Recycle Bin.
Nine characters are banned in filenames: \ / : * ? " < > | ; traditional MAX_PATH is 260 characters.
NTFS (Windows NT 3.1, 1993): journaling, permissions, compression; EFS encrypts files; BitLocker encrypts drives.
XP Home allows 5 connecting devices and XP Professional 10; the common figure for Windows 7 and later is 20.
Safe Mode is for troubleshooting; Turbo Mode is not a startup mode; Windows 10/11 recovery uses Shift + Restart.
Boot order on BIOS: bootmgr, winload.exe, ntoskrnl.exe; on UEFI: bootmgfw.efi, winload.efi, ntoskrnl.exe.
regedit = Registry, services.msc = Services, cmd.exe = Command Prompt, pagefile.sys = paging file.
Win + Z opens Snap Layouts; Shift five times starts Sticky Keys; Ctrl + F5 is a hard reload in Chrome.
